we have identified a patient with Li-Fraumenti Syndrome who has three germline mutations in the p53 gene and who has developed multiple cancers.
we identified the first child with three germline mutations in p53, and that the child had normal embryonic development despite the presence of three p53 mutations.
we have described a novel p53 compound heterozygotous mutation and that this mutation was associated with severe clinical manifestations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms of p53 function and the role of this tumor suppressor in human cancer.
the genetic basis of the Li-Fraumenie Syndrome and the functional consequences of p53 mutations on cellular growth control.
the molecular basis for the Li-Fraumenis syndrome and the development of a mouse model for this syndrome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this child has LFS and compound heterozygous mutations in p53.
the child is heterozygous for three different p53 mutations, and the clinical phenotype is consistent with LFS.
a child who has a compound heterozygous p53 mutation has a high risk of early onset cancers and a low risk of normal embryonic development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the p53 gene is not essential for embryonic development in humans, but is essential for prevention of cancer.
the p53 compound heterozygotus state in humans is not lethal, but confers a high risk of cancer.
the Li-Fraumenis Syndrome can result from a compound heterozygous state for two p53 mutations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of a second, wild-type p53 allele may be required for normal development in humans.
p53 compound heterozygosities are not necessarily associated with a severe phenotype, as is often assumed.
compound heterozygotes for p53 mutations can be identified, and the functional properties of each mutation can be determined.
